purpose: Hydroxyurea is used to treat certain types of cancer, such as chronic myelogenous leukemia and head and neck cancers. It is also commonly used to help people with sickle cell disease have fewer painful crises and serious complications. Your doctor may also use it for other blood-related conditions.
how_it_works: Hydroxyurea works by slowing down the production of abnormal or rapidly growing cells in your body. In sickle cell disease, it helps your body make a healthier type of hemoglobin — the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen — so your blood cells are less likely to become stiff and sickle-shaped. Think of it as helping your body produce better-quality blood cells that work more smoothly.
common_side_effects: The most common side effects include low blood counts (which can make you feel tired, increase your risk of infections, or cause easy bruising or bleeding), nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, mouth sores, skin rash or darkening, hair thinning, and loss of appetite. These effects are usually manageable, so let your doctor or pharmacist know if they bother you.
warnings: This medication can lower your ability to fight infections, so avoid contact with sick people and wash your hands often. It can cause serious birth defects, so do not become pregnant or father a child while taking it — use reliable birth control. Women should not breastfeed while on this medication. Long-term use may slightly increase the risk of developing certain skin cancers, so protect your skin from the sun. Your doctor will monitor your blood counts regularly while you take this medicine. Never share this medication with others.
typical_dosing: Dosing is very individual and depends on your condition, weight, and how your body responds to the medication. For sickle cell disease, adults often start at around 15 mg per kilogram of body weight once daily by mouth, and the dose may be slowly increased over time. For cancer, doses and schedules vary widely. Always take it exactly as your doctor prescribes — usually as a capsule or tablet once a day — and never change your dose without talking to your doctor first.
